title: A3 — High-performing data ingestion and transformation
bodyMarkdown:
## Data ingestion and transformation

Exam task **3.5**. Task 2.1 already covered SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and the basic shape of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams as a queuing/messaging option, and task 3.1 covered AWS DataSync and AWS Storage Gateway for hybrid storage, so this lesson refers back to both briefly and focuses on **analytics ingestion and transformation**: getting data into a data lake, moving it in batch or streaming, cataloging and transforming it, querying and visualizing it, and picking compute and access controls sized to the job.

### K01 -- Data analytics and visualization services with appropriate use cases

Three services cover most of the analytics surface tested here. **Amazon Athena** is a serverless, interactive SQL query service that runs directly against data sitting in Amazon S3 -- there is no cluster to provision, and it bills per query based on the amount of data each query scans. **AWS Lake Formation** sits a layer above raw S3: it registers S3 paths into a governed data lake and layers a **grant/revoke permissions model** on top of IAM so a data lake administrator can hand out fine-grained access to databases and tables without managing bucket policies by hand. **Amazon QuickSight** is AWS's business-intelligence service for dashboards and visuals; AWS has begun folding it into a broader **Amazon Quick** suite in its documentation, so expect to see it referenced as "Amazon Quick Sight" going forward even though the exam guide and most current docs still call it Amazon QuickSight -- functionally it is the same dashboarding service. All three plug into the same S3-backed data, at different layers: Lake Formation governs it, Athena queries it, QuickSight visualizes it.

**Exam tip:** "ad hoc SQL over files in S3, no servers to manage" is Athena; "centralize fine-grained permissions across many S3-backed tables" is Lake Formation; "interactive dashboards for business users" is QuickSight.

### K02 -- Data ingestion patterns

Ingestion splits into two patterns, and picking the right one shapes every other decision in this lesson. **Batch ingestion** collects data over a window (hourly extracts, nightly exports, a daily file drop) and loads it in one job -- simpler to build, cheaper per byte, and appropriate when the business doesn't need the data until the next report or the next day. **Streaming ingestion** delivers records continuously, often within seconds of being produced, and is required when a decision or a downstream system needs near-real-time data -- fraud scoring, live dashboards, IoT telemetry. A third pattern, **micro-batching**, buffers a stream for a short, configurable interval (seconds to minutes) before writing it out; Amazon Data Firehose (K07 below) is built around this pattern by design.

**Exam tip:** a stated tolerance for staleness ("data can be up to a day old" vs. "must reflect events within seconds") is the fastest way to tell whether a scenario wants batch or streaming.

### K03 -- Data transfer services with appropriate use cases

Task 3.1 already covered **AWS DataSync** (online, agent-based transfer from on-premises NFS/SMB/HDFS or object storage into S3, EFS, or FSx, able to saturate a 10 Gbps link) and **AWS Storage Gateway** (S3 File Gateway, Volume Gateway, and Tape Gateway for hybrid access) in depth -- see that lesson for the mechanics. For analytics ingestion specifically, the same DataSync task that lands files in S3 is often the first stage of a pipeline that a Glue crawler (K04) then catalogs and Athena or EMR (S05) then queries; DataSync's built-in checksums and metadata preservation matter here because a corrupted or incomplete landing-zone file breaks every downstream job that reads it. Recall that **AWS Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers** -- for offline, high-volume transfers AWS now points customers to DataSync for online transfer or the physical **AWS Data Transfer Terminal** facility rather than a shipped appliance.

**Exam tip:** if a question's transfer need was already solved in task 3.1 (hybrid file access, one-time bulk migration), don't re-derive it here -- just confirm the landing target (S3, typically) feeds the ingestion pipeline this lesson builds on top of it.

### K04 -- Data transformation services with appropriate use cases

**AWS Glue** is AWS's serverless data-integration service and covers three related jobs. A **Glue crawler** connects to a data source, infers its schema, and writes table definitions into the **AWS Glue Data Catalog**, a centralized metadata repository that stores the location, schema, and properties of your data sources, organized into databases and tables. Once cataloged, a **Glue ETL job** reads, transforms, and writes data at scale, in one of two engines: **Glue for Apache Spark** (distributed, for large datasets) or **Python shell** (for basic scripts on a single machine, suited for small or medium-sized datasets). **AWS Glue DataBrew** is a separate, visual data-preparation tool: a serverless, point-and-click interface with prebuilt transformations for cleaning and normalizing data -- built for analysts who want to fix data quality issues (missing values, outliers, inconsistent formats) without writing code, as opposed to a Glue ETL job, which is built for engineers who script a repeatable pipeline.

**Exam tip:** "a business analyst needs to clean messy data visually, no code" is DataBrew; "an engineer needs a repeatable, scriptable transform at scale" is a Glue ETL job; either way, the Data Catalog is what makes the result queryable by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR.

### K05 -- Secure access to ingestion access points

Every ingestion endpoint needs the same three controls layered together. **IAM policies and roles** authorize which principals can write to a Kinesis stream, an MSK cluster, a Firehose delivery stream, or an S3 landing bucket -- an ingestion pipeline should use a scoped IAM role, not long-lived static credentials, for producers and consumers alike. **Interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink)** let on-premises or in-VPC producers reach an ingestion service (Kinesis, MSK, Glue) without traversing the public internet, keeping ingestion traffic on the AWS private network. **Amazon S3 access points** add a third layer specifically for S3-based ingestion buckets shared across teams or applications: each access point is a named network endpoint attached to a bucket, with its own access point policy that works alongside the bucket policy, and can be restricted to accept requests only from a specific VPC -- an account can create up to 10,000 access points per Region, so each ingestion job gets its own narrowly scoped endpoint instead of one sprawling bucket policy.

**Exam tip:** "many applications need different, narrowly scoped access to the same ingestion bucket" points to S3 access points, not one large bucket policy; "producers inside a VPC must never cross the public internet" points to an interface VPC endpoint.

### K06 -- Sizes and speeds needed to meet business requirements

Every ingestion service exposes a throughput unit that sizing decisions revolve around. A **Kinesis Data Streams shard** supports up to 1 MiB/second or 1,000 records/second of writes and up to 2 MiB/second of reads -- add shards to scale total throughput, and split a hot key across more shards rather than adding shards blindly. **Amazon Data Firehose** buffers incoming records by size or time before delivering a batch to its destination, using configurable **buffering hints** (a size threshold and an interval, with an interval of zero meaning near-immediate delivery) -- a larger buffer produces fewer, larger delivery files (cheaper and more efficient downstream) at the cost of slightly higher end-to-end latency. **Amazon MSK** sizing is a broker decision: pick broker instance type, count, and storage to match sustained throughput, durability (replication factor), and availability needs, or skip broker sizing entirely with **MSK Serverless**, which automatically provisions and scales capacity and bills on a throughput basis. **AWS DataSync** throughput is bounded by the agent's network link, not the service itself -- a single task can saturate a 10 Gbps connection (task 3.1).

**Exam tip:** a scenario that names a specific records-per-second or MiB/second figure is testing shard math (records/second and MiB/second against the 1,000/1 MiB write limit per shard) -- divide the stated load by the per-shard limit to get a minimum shard count.

### K07 -- Streaming data services with appropriate use cases

Task 2.1 introduced **Amazon Kinesis Data Streams** as an ordered, replayable stream multiple independent consumers can read at their own pace. Three more services complete the streaming picture, and telling them apart is a frequent exam point. **Amazon Data Firehose** (renamed from Kinesis Data Firehose) is the fully managed delivery service: it buffers and loads streaming data into a destination -- S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Splunk, or a generic HTTP endpoint -- with little to no code, optionally transforming records with a Lambda function along the way; it has no shards to manage and no data to replay, because once delivered a record is gone from Firehose. **Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink** (renamed from Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink) is a managed runtime for building custom stream-processing applications in SQL, Java, Python, or Scala -- windowed aggregations, joins across streams, anomaly detection -- code Firehose cannot express. **Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka)** is a managed, Apache Kafka-compatible cluster for teams that already use Kafka's ecosystem and client libraries; unlike Kinesis Data Streams' proprietary API, MSK exposes the standard Kafka protocol, so existing Kafka producers, consumers, and connectors run against it largely unchanged.

**Exam tip:** "just land the stream in S3/Redshift, no custom logic" is Firehose; "need custom windowed computation over the stream" is Managed Service for Apache Flink; "already runs on open-source Apache Kafka" is MSK; "need multiple independent consumers to replay the same ordered stream" is Kinesis Data Streams.

### S01 -- Building and securing data lakes

Assemble a data lake from the pieces above in order: land raw data in **Amazon S3** (via DataSync, Firehose, or a direct write), **register** the relevant S3 paths with **AWS Lake Formation** so they become part of the governed data lake, run a **Glue crawler** to populate the **Glue Data Catalog** with the schema, and grant access through Lake Formation's grant/revoke permission model rather than individual S3 bucket policies -- Lake Formation permissions augment IAM rather than replacing it, and a single **data lake administrator** is designated first to hand out narrower permissions afterward. **Hybrid access mode** lets a team migrate to Lake Formation permissions gradually, securing some tables with Lake Formation while others still rely on IAM and S3 permissions directly, so an existing pipeline isn't forced to convert all at once. Store raw and transformed data in separate prefixes or buckets (a common "raw / curated / enriched" layering) so a bad transform never overwrites the source of truth.

**Exam tip:** "many teams need centrally managed, fine-grained access to the same catalog of tables" is Lake Formation's grant/revoke model, not a patchwork of S3 bucket policies.

### S02 -- Designing data streaming architectures

Chain K07's services by role: a producer (application, IoT device, database change stream) writes into **Kinesis Data Streams** or **MSK** for durable, ordered, replayable ingestion; **Amazon Data Firehose** (optionally reading from that same Kinesis stream) delivers a copy to S3 for the data lake with format conversion and compression along the way; and **Managed Service for Apache Flink** reads from the stream in parallel to run real-time aggregations or alerts, all without interfering with each other because Kinesis Data Streams supports multiple independent readers. Decide up front whether consumers need **enhanced fan-out** (each registered consumer gets its own dedicated 2 MiB/second per shard) or can share the shard's base 2 MiB/second read throughput -- a design with several consumers competing for shared throughput risks starving one of them under load.

**Exam tip:** "one stream, several independent downstream consumers, each needing guaranteed throughput" calls for enhanced fan-out consumers, not a single shared reader.

### S03 -- Designing data transfer solutions

Match the transfer requirement to the right service rather than defaulting to one option: a **one-time or periodic bulk load** from an on-premises file system into S3 is AWS DataSync; **persistent hybrid file or block access** with a local cache is AWS Storage Gateway (task 3.1); a **continuous stream of application events** is Kinesis Data Streams, MSK, or Firehose (K07); and a **very large, offline transfer with no viable network path** now points to the physical AWS Data Transfer Terminal facility, since Snowball Edge no longer accepts new customers. For a design that needs both a hybrid presence and eventual analytics, DataSync or Storage Gateway typically lands the data in S3 first, and the ingestion services in this lesson pick it up from there -- the transfer choice and the analytics choice are usually two separate decisions joined at the S3 bucket.

**Exam tip:** don't reach for a streaming service to solve a bulk file-transfer requirement, or for DataSync to solve a live event stream -- match the data's shape (file vs. continuous events) to the service family first.

### S04 -- Implementing visualization strategies

**Amazon QuickSight** connects to data sources (S3 via Athena, Redshift, RDS, and others), lets an author prepare a dataset (filtering, renaming fields, adding calculated fields), and publishes the result as an interactive **dashboard** that other users view and filter without seeing the underlying query. For datasets an author queries repeatedly, importing them into **SPICE** (QuickSight's in-memory calculation engine) avoids re-querying the source on every interaction, trading a refresh step for materially faster, more scalable dashboards under concurrent use. When the underlying data lives in S3 as raw files, the usual chain is: Glue crawler catalogs it, Athena (or Redshift Spectrum) exposes it as queryable tables, and QuickSight connects to Athena as its data source -- QuickSight itself does not query raw S3 files directly. Choose a direct-query dataset over SPICE when the dashboard must reflect data as of the last write rather than the last scheduled refresh.

**Exam tip:** "dashboard must reflect the freshest possible data on every load" argues against SPICE's imported/refreshed mode in favor of direct query; "hundreds of concurrent viewers, dataset changes only periodically" argues for SPICE.

### S05 -- Selecting appropriate compute options for data processing

Four compute options cover most processing needs, ordered roughly by how much infrastructure they expose. **Amazon Athena** needs no compute to manage at all -- point it at cataloged S3 data and it runs ad hoc SQL, serverless. **AWS Glue** ETL jobs (K04) run serverless Spark or Python shell transforms without a cluster to size. **Amazon EMR Serverless** runs the same open-source big-data frameworks (Spark, Hive, Presto/Trino) as classic EMR without provisioning or sizing a cluster, scaling automatically to the job. **Amazon EMR** (cluster mode) is the choice when a workload needs a long-lived, tunable, multi-node Hadoop/Spark cluster -- heavy, sustained big-data processing, custom cluster software, or fine-grained control over instance types and count that the serverless options don't expose. Move down this list (from serverless toward a managed cluster) only when a stated requirement -- sustained heavy load, custom software, or fine-grained tuning -- can't be met by the simpler, more managed option above it.

**Exam tip:** "occasional SQL over files in S3" is Athena; "scriptable ETL, no cluster to manage" is Glue; "run existing Spark/Hive jobs without managing a cluster" is EMR Serverless; "need to tune or customize a persistent big-data cluster" is EMR.

### S06 -- Selecting appropriate configurations for ingestion

Configuration follows directly from the pattern chosen in K02 and the sizing in K06: a batch job is configured by its **schedule** (hourly, nightly) and its **file format** at write time (K04/S07); a streaming pipeline is configured by **shard count** (Kinesis Data Streams, sized to the required MiB/second and records/second), **buffering hints** (Firehose, trading latency for larger, cheaper delivery files), and **broker sizing or serverless mode** (MSK). Partition keys matter for both patterns: a Kinesis Data Streams partition key that is too uniform overloads a single shard, and an S3 landing-zone **partition scheme** (by date, region, or another high-cardinality, evenly distributed field) determines how efficiently Athena and Glue can later prune data instead of scanning an entire dataset.

**Exam tip:** ingestion configuration questions usually give you either a throughput number (pick shard count or a Firehose buffer size) or a downstream query pattern (pick a partition key) -- work backward from whichever one the stem states.

### S07 -- Transforming data between formats

Converting row-based, text formats (CSV, JSON) into **columnar formats** (Apache Parquet, Apache ORC) is one of the highest-value transforms in this lesson, because Athena and other engines charge and perform based on how much data a query scans -- and a columnar format lets a query read only the columns it needs. In one AWS-published cost-modeling example, querying the same un-partitioned dataset stored as CSV versus Parquet dropped the data scanned from 102.9 GB to 1.04 GB and the query time from 4 minutes 20 seconds to under 13 seconds -- AWS describes this as **"a saving of 99% and improved performance by 95%"** -- because Parquet's columnar layout means a query reads only the columns and byte ranges it needs. This conversion is typically done as a **Glue ETL job** (Spark, reading CSV and writing partitioned Parquet) or as an **Athena CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS)** query that reads an existing table and writes a new one in Parquet or ORC -- either approach also benefits from writing the output already partitioned (S06) so downstream queries prune data twice: once by not scanning unneeded columns, and once by not scanning unneeded partitions.

**Exam tip:** "queries over raw CSV/JSON in S3 are slow and expensive" points to converting to Parquet or ORC (via a Glue job or an Athena CTAS), not to a bigger Athena workgroup or more compute.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
